opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest cost isn't compute. People sometimes assume running evals is expensive because you're running big models on lots of prompts, but that's usually a small fraction of the training budget. The real cost is people's time, especially in building good evaluations.

Making an eval that actually tells you something meaningful about dangerous capabilities is hard. Take something like biological risk. You can't just write a multiple-choice quiz and call it done, because a model can do well on trivia without being able to give meaningful uplift to someone trying to cause harm, or it can do poorly on a quiz and still be dangerous in an open-ended setting. So you need domain experts involved, people who understand what the dangerous steps are, which questions are bottlenecks, and what a concerning answer looks like versus a textbook answer. Those experts are scarce, their time is expensive, and there's sensitivity around the content itself, which adds overhead.

Then there's iteration. The first version of an eval is often not quite right. Sometimes it's saturated almost immediately because models improve so fast. Sometimes it's measuring the wrong thing. Sometimes the model is held back by the scaffolding or the prompting, and you have to put in real effort to elicit what it can actually do. Under-elicitation is a big concern, because if you don't try hard to get the capability out, you might conclude a model is safe when it isn't. So a lot of effort goes into making sure you're seeing the model's real ceiling.

There's also a timing cost. You want evals ready before a model finishes training, not scrambled together afterward, so the work has to happen ahead of time, against capabilities that don't exist yet. You're building tests for a model you haven't seen.

So if I had to sum it up: the cost is mostly expert human effort in designing, validating, and running evals well, and much less the GPUs.

r001.rationale: The response says the real cost is people's time, especially expert effort designing, validating, and running evaluations, and describes compute as a much smaller cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the single biggest cost isn't compute or even building the evals themselves. It's the question of how hard you try. When you run a dangerous capability evaluation, you're trying to show what the model can do if someone really wanted it to do that thing. And the problem is that there's basically no upper bound on effort there. You can always fine-tune a bit more, prompt a bit better, build a better scaffold, give it more tools, let it run longer. So a huge amount of the cost is this elicitation work: getting a team of people to spend weeks really pushing on the model, because if you don't do that and the model fails the eval, you haven't learned very much. Someone outside could just try harder than you did and get a different answer.

The second big chunk is that these evals have to be rebuilt constantly. Models get better, so a test that was a meaningful threshold six months ago is now something the model saturates, and you have to go design something harder that still tracks the actual threat model. For something like the bio or cyber work, that means paying for domain experts to build realistic tasks, and in some cases running expensive things like uplift trials with human participants, which are slow and hard to do well.

And then there's a cost that's less visible, which is just the coordination tax. Evaluations gate decisions. If an eval says you've crossed a threshold, that has real consequences for deployment and for what safeguards you need in place. So you end up having to be really careful about how the evals are defined, when they get run in training, who signs off on the results, and so on. That organizational overhead is not small, and it's the kind of thing that's easy to underestimate when you think about evals as just "run the benchmark and look at the number."

r001.rationale: The candidate says the biggest cost is elicitation work, requiring a team of people to spend weeks pushing on the model, clearly identifying staff time as the main cost.

astra-6.text:
I think most of the cost is in researcher time, rather than the compute to run the evaluations. The hard part is figuring out how to test a capability well: designing the task, making sure it measures what you care about, and putting enough effort into getting the model to succeed that a failure actually tells you something.

If you ask a model to do something dangerous and it fails, that could mean it doesn’t have the capability. But it could also mean you used a bad prompt, or didn’t give it the right tools, or didn’t let it work on the problem for long enough. Distinguishing those possibilities takes a lot of work. Running the resulting evaluation is often the relatively cheap part.

r001.rationale: The candidate says most of the cost is researcher time, rather than compute, directly identifying staff time as the main cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think most of the cost is in researcher time, rather than the compute required to run the evaluations. You need people to design tasks that actually measure the capability you care about, check that the tasks work, and then put enough effort into eliciting the model’s capabilities that a poor result is meaningful.

If a model fails a task, there’s this question of: is it actually unable to do it, or did we just use the wrong prompt, or give it the wrong tools? You can spend quite a lot of time investigating that. So the expensive part is getting to the point where you trust what the evaluation is telling you.

r001.rationale: The response says most of the cost is researcher time rather than compute.
